quote: Service Entrance Sub-distribution Terminal Equipment Installation point (e.g. Main distribution board or telecom (e.g. socket outlet) board or telecom NTP) PBX frame Mains Test VI IV2 IIV3 Class/SPD Type ( 1) Surge test waveform 10/350 current 8/20 current Combination 8/20 current and 1.2/50 voltage Typical peak test 25kA (2) 40kA 3kA (with 6kV)

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): transient overvoltage SPDs (Type 2/3) protect against indirect lightning and switching transients and should be installed at sub-distribution boards and at equipment level for critical equipment.
quote: Designed to protect electrical/electronic equipment from the secondary eﬀects of indirect lightning and against switching transients. SPDs should be installed at sub-distribution boards and at equipment level for critical equipment.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): all incoming services (metallic water and gas pipes, power and data cables) should be bonded to a single earth reference point, which may be the main earthing terminal or a bonding ring conductor.
quote: As Figure 23 illustrates, all incoming services (metallic water and gas pipes, power and data cables) should be bonded to a single earth reference point. This equipotential bonding bar may be the main earthing terminal, a bonding ring conductor or a partial ring conductor inside the outer walls of the structure.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): the armouring of power and telecom cables can be bonded directly to the main earthing bar at the service entrance, but the live conductors within these cables cannot be bonded directly to earth.
quote: The armouring of metallic electrical services such as power and telecommunication lines can be directly bonded to the main earthing bar at the service entrance. However the live conductors within these service cables cannot be directly bonded to earth.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018), quoting BS EN 62305-4: Type 1 SPDs alone provide no effective protection against failure of sensitive electrical or electronic systems; Type 2 and Type 3 SPDs are also needed.
quote: However, the use of these Type 1 SPDs alone “provides no eﬀective protection against failure of sensitive electrical or electronic systems”

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): where a structural lightning protection system is required, lightning current (equipotential bonding) SPDs are always required on every metallic electrical service entering the structure: mains Type 1 and data/telecom Category D.
quote: If the risk evaluation demands that a structural LPS is required then equipotential bonding or lightning current SPDs are always required for any metallic electrical service entering the structure (typically power and telecom lines where mains Type 1 SPDs and signal/data Category D tested SPDs are used respectively).

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): for a worst-case 200 kA strike with a single three-phase power service, 50% (100 kA) is assumed to flow through the power line and share equally over 4 conductors, so each L-E and N-E SPD sees 25 kA (10/350).
quote: 50% or 100kA of the total lightning current is discharged through the power line. This is assumed to share equally between the 4 conductors within the power line, thus each SPD between line and earth and neutral and earth would be subject to 25kA (ie 100kA/4).

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): the worst-case surge expected on a two-wire telephone or data line is 2.5 kA (10/350) per line to earth (Category D test) or 5 kA per pair.
quote: the worst case surge that could be expected on a two-wire telephone or data line is 2.5kA (10/350µs) per line (Category D test to BS EN 61643-21) to earth or 5kA (10/350µs) per pair.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): where no structural LPS is required but a service arrives by overhead line, lightning current SPDs are needed: 12.5 kA 10/350 per mode for mains Type 1 and 2.5 kA 10/350 per mode for signal/telecom SPDs.
quote: any electrical services feeding the structure via an overhead line will require lightning current SPDs. For mains Type 1 SPDs the surge current rating per mode of protection is 12.5kA 10/350µs and for signal/telecom SPDs the surge current rating per mode of protection is 2.5kA 10/350µs.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): underground services without a structural LPS do not need lightning current SPDs; overvoltage (Type 2 / Category C) SPDs are sufficient.
quote: Underground electrical services therefore do not have a requirement for lightning current SPDs where no structural LPS is present – overvoltage SPDs are suﬃcient to provide eﬀective protection.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): poor coordination can expose a downstream overvoltage SPD to excess surge energy; appropriate SPDs should be fitted wherever services cross from one lightning protection zone to another.
quote: Poor coordination could mean that an overvoltage SPD is subjected to an excess of surge energy placing both itself and connected equipment at risk from damage. Appropriate SPDs should be ﬁtted wherever services cross from one LPZ to another.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): if the distance from an SPD to the protected equipment is over 10 m, oscillations could double the voltage at the equipment.
quote: oscillation protective distance – if the distance from the SPD to the equipment is over 10m, oscillations could lead to a doubling of voltage

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018) Table 5 (as BS 7671 Table 443.2) for 230/240 V: category IV 6 kV (electricity meter), III 4 kV (distribution board), II 2.5 kV (sub-distribution board / electrical equipment), I 1.5 kV (socket outlet / electronic equipment).
quote: IV (equipment with very 6kV Electricity meter high overvoltage impulse) withstand III (equipment with high 4kV Distribution board overvoltage impulse) withstand II (equipment with normal 2.5kV Sub-distribution board/ overvoltage impulse) Electrical equipment withstand I (equipment with reduced 1.5kV Socket outlet/

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018), citing BS 7671 443.1.1 Note 4: transient overvoltages transmitted by the supply system are not significantly attenuated downstream in most installations.
quote: This concurs with BS 7671 443.1.1 Note 4 which states ‘Transient overvoltages transmitted by the supply distribution system are not signiﬁcantly attenuated downstream in most installations’.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018 443.6.2): Category I equipment connected to the fixed installation must be protected against transient overvoltages, e.g. by an SPD installed external to the equipment.
quote: However clause 443.6.2 makes it clear if Category I equipment is to be connected to the ﬁxed electrical installation, it must be protected against transient overvoltages. An SPD installed external to this equipment serves this purpose.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): because electronic equipment has sensitive components connected between live conductors, SPDs with differential-mode (L-N) protection should be selected for it.
quote: Diﬀerential mode transients, also due to electrical switching events, which present particular problems for electronic equipment where their sensitive electronic components are connected between live conductors and hence SPDs with diﬀerential mode protection should be selected to protect such equipment.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): supply-authority rules often prevent service-entrance (Type 1) SPDs being installed upstream of the electricity meter, so they are fitted at the main distribution board.
quote: Often due to power supply authority regulations, the application of SPDs at the service entrance (typically the equipotential bonding Type 1 SPDs) cannot be installed upstream or before the electricity meter. Such SPDs are therefore ﬁtted at the main distribution board.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): a Type 1 SPD at the main distribution board (category III) must keep the voltage protection level well below the 4 kV rated impulse voltage to prevent flashover.
quote: Conventionally the main distribution board falls within overvoltage impulse category III (see Table 5), the installed mains Type 1 SPD must ensure that during lightning activity, the voltage protection level is well below the rated impulse voltage value of 4kV to prevent dangerous sparking through insulation breakdown caused by ﬂashover.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): terminal equipment at socket outlets is category I (1.5 kV), and a Type 3 SPD (Class III test, 6 kV 1.2/50 and 3 kA 8/20) is typically employed at that location.
quote: rated impulse voltage of 1.5kV. An overvoltage mains Type 3 SPD (tested with the Class III test to BS EN 61643 which is a combination or hybrid waveform of 6kV (1.2/50µs voltage) and 3kA (8/20µs current) is typically employed at this location

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): lead inductance is taken as 1 µH/m, so an impulse current rising at 1 kA/µs adds approximately 1 kV per metre of SPD connecting lead.
quote: As a general rule, the lead inductance (L) is assumed to be 1 µH/m. This inductive voltage drop, when caused by an impulse current with a rate of rise of 1 kA/µs will be approximately 1 kV/m of lead length.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): SPD connecting leads shall be as short as possible, preferably not exceeding 0.5 m total lead length (l1 + l2).
quote: Therefore in order to achieve optimum overvoltage protection, connecting leads of SPDs shall be as short as possible, preferably not exceeding 0,5 m for the total lead length (l1 + l2 see Figure 30).

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): SPD connecting leads should also be tightly bound together over as much of their length as possible (cable ties or spiral wrap) to cancel inductance.
quote: In addition to keeping connecting leads short, they should be tightly bound together over as much of their length as possible, using cable ties or spiral wrap.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): in a 6 kV/3 kA test an SPD with Up 600 V fitted with its recommended 25 cm of bound connecting lead gave 630 V overall.
quote: The SPD therefore has a protection level Up of 600V when measured across its terminals with a 6kV/3kA surge test. If this protector is ﬁtted with its recommended length (25 cm in this case) of bound connecting lead, the overall voltage of the SPD plus connecting leads is 630V as shown in Figure 33 graph.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): with unbound connecting leads the same SPD let through 810 V with 25 cm leads and 2,300 V with 2 m leads.
quote: If these connecting leads are left unbound, then the overall voltage rises to 810V with the recommended connecting leads (25 cm), and to 2,300V with the 2 m leads.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): where the SPD earth lead would be long, in metal enclosures use two earth conductors: one closely connected to the enclosure metalwork and one to the earth bar, which is itself connected directly to the metal of the assembly.
quote: For metal cabinets and enclosures one conductor should be closely connected to the metalwork of the assembly, whilst the other should be connected directly to the earth bar. This, in turn, should be connected directly to the metal of the assembly.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): series (in-line) SPDs, used for low-current power (typically 16 A or less), telecom, data and signal lines, are not affected by connecting lead length, but their earthing conductor must be kept as short as possible.
quote: Low current SPDs for power (typically 16A or less), telecommunication, data and signal equipment are usually installed in series (in-line) with the equipment they are protecting and are not aﬀected by length of their connecting leads. However, the earthing conductors of series SPDs must be kept as short as possible as shown in Figure 34

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): oscillation (voltage doubling) may be disregarded for cable runs of less than 10 m from the SPD.
quote: Oscillations may be disregarded for cable runs of less than 10m from the SPD. Some terminal equipment may have internal protective components for EMC purposes (for example Metal Oxide Varistors or MOVs) that will signiﬁcantly reduce oscillations even at longer distances.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): Type 1 (lightning current) SPDs protect against common-mode surges, connected line to earth and neutral to earth on TN systems.
quote: Equipotential bonding or lightning current SPDs protect against common mode surges. On a power supply for example, Type 1 SPDs protect between line to earth, and neutral to earth on TN earthing systems to prevent dangerous sparking.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): terminal equipment is more vulnerable to differential-mode surges, and downstream overvoltage SPDs protect against both common- and differential-mode surges.
quote: Terminal equipment tends to be more vulnerable to diﬀerential mode surges. Downstream overvoltage SPDs protect against both common and diﬀerential mode surges

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): on a 230 V supply a service-entrance Type 1 SPD should have a voltage protection level of no more than 1600 V.
quote: For example, in the case of a 230V mains supply a Type 1 SPD ﬁtted at the service entrance (for lightning equipotential bonding) should have a voltage protection level of no more than 1600V when tested in accordance with BS EN 61643 series (Class I Test).

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): to allow for lead voltage and possible doubling, overvoltage SPDs should have a voltage protection level of no more than 600 V (1.5 kV x 0.8 / 2) in the Class III test.
quote: overvoltage SPDs should have a voltage protection level of no more than 600V ((1.5kV x 0.8)/2) when tested in accordance with BS EN 61643 series (Class III test).

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018): Section 534 requires installed SPDs to be protected against short-circuit by overcurrent protective devices (OCPDs).
quote: BS 7671 Section 534 requires installed SPDs to be protected against short-circuit through the use of over current protective devices (OCPDs).

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018 Section 534): SPD connecting cables shall be at least 16 mm2 copper for Type 1 SPDs and 4 mm2 copper for Type 2 and Type 3 SPDs (or not less than the line conductor where that is below 4 mm2).
quote: minimum cross-sectional areas of 16mm2 (copper) for the high energy Type 1 SPD and 4mm2 (copper) for Type 2 and Type 3 SPDs if the cross-sectional area of the line conductors is > 4mm2, or not less than that of the line conductor, where the line conductors have a cross- sectional area less than 4mm2.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): mains SPDs have internal overload (typically thermal) disconnection, so their connecting conductors need only short-circuit protection by an OCPD in line with the connecting cables.
quote: In the event of an overload fault condition, BS EN 61643 SPD product test standards require mains power SPDs to have internal overload protection (typically a thermal disconnection). The connecting conductors to SPDs therefore need only be protected against short-circuit fault conditions by the use of an OCPD in-line with the connecting cables

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018) Figure 37: the preferred position for a parallel SPD with its dedicated OCPD is the outgoing way closest to the incomer.
quote: 1. main switch/isolator 4 2. main supply OCPD 3. preferred outgoing way OCPD (closest to incomer) 4. alternative outgoing way for SPD with dedicated OCPD OCPD 5. SPD with dedicated OCPD

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): a typical Type 2 SPD rated 40 kA 8/20 is likely to state a maximum OCPD of 125 A and may recommend 10 mm2 connecting cables.
quote: For example, a typical (industry common) Type 2 SPD with a peak surge current of 40kA 8/20 is likely to state a maximum OCPD rating of 125A and may recommend 10mm2 connecting cables.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): the maximum OCPD rating declared by the SPD manufacturer must never be exceeded.
quote: It is important to ensure that the maximum OCPD rating declared by the SPD manufacturer is never exceeded.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): where upstream OCPD characteristics are not available (e.g. retrofit), the SPD's OCPD may be rated at half the nominal value of the immediate upstream OCPD to achieve discrimination.
quote: Where manufacturer’s operating characteristics for the upstream OCPD are not available, for example a retroﬁt installation, it may be safely assumed that the OCPD for the SPD should be rated at half the nominal value of the immediate upstream OCPD.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018 534.2.3.4.1): Section 534 requires a minimum nominal discharge current In of 5 kA 8/20 for each mode of protection in the common CT1 configuration.
quote: Section 534 requires a minimum Inspd of 5kA 8/20 for each SPD mode of protection on the common CT1 conﬁguration (534.2.3.4.1).

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): SPDs should wherever possible be installed upstream of RCDs to prevent unwanted RCD tripping caused by transient overvoltages.
quote: SPDs should wherever possible be installed upstream of RCDs to prevent unwanted tripping caused by transient overvoltages.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018 534.2.1): where SPDs are on the load side of an RCD, the RCD shall have a surge-current immunity of at least 3 kA 8/20; S-type RCDs satisfy this.
quote: Where SPDs are installed in accordance with BS 7671 534.2.1 and are on the load side of a residual current device, an RCD having an immunity to surge currents of at least 3 kA 8/20, shall be used. NOTE 1: S-type RCDs satisfy this requirement.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): if the SPD is downstream of the RCD, the RCD should be a time-delayed type with surge immunity of at least 3 kA 8/20.
quote: If the SPD is installed downstream of the RCD, the RCD should be of the time delayed type with an immunity to surge currents of at least 3kA 8/20.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018 534.2.2): connection type CT1 is used for TN-C-S/TN-S systems and for TT systems where the SPD is downstream of the RCD.
quote: An SPD conﬁguration based on Connection Type 1 (CT1) is for TN-C-S/TN-S earthing arrangements as well the TT earthing arrangement where the SPD is ﬁtted downstream of the RCD.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018): connection type CT2 is required on a TT system if the SPD is upstream of the RCD, because the downstream RCD would not operate if the SPD became defective.
quote: An SPD conﬁguration based on Connection Type 2 (CT2) is required on a TT earth arrangement if the SPD is upstream of the RCD. The RCD being downstream of the SPD would not operate should the SPD become defective.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): a defective CT2 line-to-neutral SPD creates a short-circuit rather than an earth-fault current, so its in-line OCPD operates within the required disconnection time.
quote: Should the SPD become defective it would therefore create a short-circuit current rather than an earth fault current and as such would ensure that the OCPD in-line with the SPD safely operates within the required disconnection time.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): in CT2 a higher-energy SPD, typically a spark gap for Type 1, is used between neutral and the protective conductor because it sees up to 4 times the surge current of the line-to-neutral SPDs.
quote: A higher energy SPD is used between neutral and the protective conductor. This higher energy SPD (typically a spark-gap for a Type 1 SPD) is required as lightning currents arise towards the protective conductor and as such this higher energy SPD sees up to 4 times the surge current of the SPDs connected between the live conductors.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018): if Iimp cannot be calculated, the N-PE SPD in a 3-phase CT2 installation is at least 50 kA 10/350 (4 x 12.5 kA of the L-N SPDs); CT2 is often called the '3+1' arrangement.
quote: Iimp cannot be calculated, 534.2.3.4.3 advises that the minimum value Iimp for an SPD between neutral and the protective conductor is 50kA 10/350 for a 3 phase CT2 installation, 4 times 12.5kA 10/350 of the SPDs between the live conductors. The CT2 SPD conﬁguration is often referred the ‘3+1’ arrangement for a 3 phase supply.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): technically, if SPDs are within 0.5 m of the PEN split into N and PE, no N-PE protection mode is needed.
quote: From a technical point of view, if SPDs are applied within a 0.5m distance of the PEN split to separate N and PE, there is no need to have an SPD protection mode between N and PE as shown

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): because UK SPDs can only be installed on the consumer side of a TN-C-S system, normally at the main board more than 0.5 m from the PEN split, an N-PE SPD is needed as in a TN-S system.
quote: the distance between the SPD installation point and the PEN split will almost always be greater than 0.5m so there is a need to have an SPD between N and PE as required for a TN-S system.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018): for Section 534, TN-C-S (PME) systems are treated the same as TN-S systems for selection and installation of SPDs.
quote: In summary, as far as Section 534 is concerned, TN-C-S systems are treated the same as TN-S systems for the selection and installation of SPDs.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018) Figure 40: if the cable length between SPD types is short (per manufacturer's data), a decoupling element is used to provide inductance for correct coordination.
quote: NOTE: If the cable length between the SPD types is short (refer to manufacturers’ data), a decoupling element is employed to provide inductance for correct SPD co-ordination

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): an SPD at the main intake panel or a distribution board should have a separate overcurrent protective device, depending on the prospective fault current there.
quote: Where installed at the main intake switch panel or a distribution board the Surge Protection Device (SPD) should have a separate overcurrent protection device (OCPD), depending on the maximum prospective fault current at the point of installation.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): provision should be made for readily disconnecting the neutral conductors for testing, by 2-pole or 4-pole means of isolation.
quote: It is recommended that provision should be made for readily disconnecting the neutral conductors for testing purposes this should be achieved by 2-pole or 4-pole means of isolation.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): the total length L1 + L2 + L3 of SPD connections to the network and the earth terminal block should not exceed 50 cm.
quote: The total length (L = L1 + L2 + L3) of SPD connections to the network and the earth terminal block should not exceed 50 cm

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018): where SPDs are installed, a durable notice complying with BS 7671 should be fixed adjacent to the distribution board(s).
quote: Where SPDs are installed a durable notice should be ﬁxed adjacent to the distribution board(s) and equipment complying with the requirements of BS 7671.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018 612.3.2): where an SPD cannot practically be disconnected (e.g. a fixed surge-protected socket outlet), insulation resistance is tested at 250 V between live conductors and earth.
quote: Where it is not practical to disconnect the SPD (e.g. a ﬁxed surge protected socket outlet), a 250V test should be applied between live conductors and Earth in accordance with BS 7671 Regulation 612.3.2.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): SPDs should be isolated during insulation resistance testing because they may operate on the test voltage.
quote: WARNING : – SPDs should be isolated during insulation resistance testing, as the SPD could operate, by treating the test voltage applied to the system as a transient overvoltage, thus defeating the object of the test.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): periodic inspection first checks that the SPD's OCPD has not operated and that the SPD's fault indicator shows it serviceable.
quote: Check that the OCPD has not operated and that the SPD is still in a serviceable condition. (SPDs have fault indicators that will show when the device has been damaged or destroyed by a surge).

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): during periodic testing, with the SPD's OCPD open a 500 V insulation resistance test is applied between live conductors and earth, expecting more than 1 megohm (BS 7671 Table 61).
quote: With the OCPD in the open position apply a 500V insulation resistance test between live conductors and earth. The resistance value should be >1MD, see BS 7671 Table 61.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): visual inspection of a surge protection system should verify that bonding conductors and cable shields are intact and cable segregation is maintained.
quote: Visual inspections are very important, and should verify, for example, if bonding conductors and cable shields are intact and appropriate cable arrangements (segregation, etc) are maintained.
section: 11 Inspection and maintenance of an SPM system

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018): inspection should catch later additions such as a power line to external CCTV cameras or car-park lighting that crosses a lightning protection zone and needs an SPD.
quote: For example, a power supply line to external CCTV cameras or car park lighting may have been added as this line is likely to cross an LPZ. Suitable protection measures (e.g. SPD) should be employed to ensure the integrity of the complete SPM is not compromised.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018 Section 443): if there is a risk of a direct lightning strike to the structure or to overhead lines feeding it, SPDs are required per BS EN 62305.
quote: Outside of such high risk installations, if there is a risk of direct lightning strike to the structure itself or to overhead lines to the structure SPDs will be required in accordance with BS EN62305.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018 443.4): for a single dwelling unit the designer should complete a documented assessment of whether the installation and equipment value justifies SPDs or the consequential losses are tolerable.
quote: This means that the electrical installation designer should complete a documented assessment for single dwelling units to determine if the total value of the electrical installation and the equipment connected therein necessitates the cost of SPDs or if the consequential losses are tolerable.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, 2018), citing IEC 60364-4-44: overvoltage protection is not required for a single dwelling where the total economic value of the installation is less than five times the value of the SPD at the origin.
quote: This is further explained in IEC 60364-4-44 which states that overvoltage protection is not required for single dwelling units where the total economic value of the electrical installation to be protected is less than ﬁve times the economic value of the SPD located at the origin of the installation.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018 443.5): if the calculated risk level CRL is less than 1000 SPD protection shall be installed; at 1000 or higher it is not required.
quote: If the CRL value is less than 1000 (or less than a 1 in 1000th chance) then SPD protection shall be installed. Similarly if the CRL value is 1000 or higher (or greater than a 1 in 1000th chance) then SPD protection is not required for the installation.

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018): in CRL = fenv / (Lp x Ng) the environmental factor fenv is 85 for rural and suburban and 850 for urban locations.
quote: Rural Area with a low Countryside 85 density of buildings Suburban Area with a medium Town outskirts 85 density of buildings Urban Area with a high Town centre 850

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018): the risk assessment length is Lp = 2 LPAL + LPCL + 0.4 LPAH + 0.2 LPCH (km), weighting low-voltage overhead line most heavily.
quote: LP = 2 LPAL + LPCL + 0.4 LPAH + 0.2 LPCH (km) where: LPAL is the length (km) of low-voltage overhead line; LPCL is the length (km) of low-voltage underground cable; LPAH is the length (km) of high-voltage overhead line; LPCH is the length (km) of high-voltage underground cable

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018 534.4.1.3): where the structure has an external LPS or needs protection against direct lightning on overhead lines, Type 1 SPDs shall be installed as close as possible to the origin of the installation.
quote: Where the structure is equipped with an external lightning protection system LPS or protection against the effects of direct lightning on overhead lines Type 1 SPDs shall be installed as close as possible to the origin of the electrical installation. (534.4.1.3)

claim: BEAMA SPD guide (UK, BS 7671:2018 534.4.1.1): SPDs installed close to sensitive equipment against internally generated switching transients shall be Type 2 or Type 3.
quote: SPDs installed close to sensitive equipment to further protect against (443.4) switching transients originating within the building shall be Type 2 or Type 3. (534.4.1.1)

claim: Schneider Electrical Installation Guide: the length of the SPD connections between the network (via the external short-circuit protective device) and the earthing terminal block should not exceed 50 cm.
quote: The first rule to comply with is that the length of the SPD connections between the network (via the external SCPD) and the earthing terminal block should not exceed 50 cm.

claim: Schneider Electrical Installation Guide: protected outgoing feeders should be connected to the terminals of the external SCPD or the SPD and physically separated from the polluted incoming conductors.
quote: The conductors of protected outgoing feeders: should be connected to the terminals of the external SCPD or the SPD; should be separated physically from the polluted incoming conductors.

claim: Schneider Electrical Installation Guide: the incoming phase, neutral and PE conductors should run beside one another to reduce loop area.
quote: The incoming feeder phase, neutral and protection (PE) conductors should run one beside another in order to reduce the loop surface

claim: Schneider Electrical Installation Guide: the SPD's incoming conductors should be kept remote from the protected outgoing conductors to avoid polluting them by coupling.
quote: The incoming conductors of the SPD should be remote from the protected outgoing conductors to avoid polluting them by coupling

claim: Schneider Electrical Installation Guide: cables should be pinned against the metal parts of the enclosure to minimise loop area, and switchboard and enclosure frames must be earthed via very short connections.
quote: The cables should be pinned against the metallic parts of the enclosure (if any) in order to minimize the surface of the frame loop and hence benefit from a shielding effect against EM disturbances. In all cases, it must be checked that the frames of switchboards and enclosures are earthed via very short connections.

claim: Schneider Electrical Installation Guide: SPD connection conductors have about 1 µH/m, so an 8 kA 8/20 µs current creates a voltage rise of 1000 V per metre of cable.
quote: For high-frequency currents, the impedance per unit length of this connection is approximately 1 µH/m. Hence, applying Lenz's law to this connection: ΔU = L di/dt The normalized 8/20 µs current wave, with a current amplitude of 8 kA, accordingly creates a voltage rise of 1000 V per metre of cable.

claim: Schneider Electrical Installation Guide: with 50 cm total connections and an 8 kA 8/20 µs surge, the voltage across the equipment terminals is Up + 500 V.
quote: If L1+L2+L3 = 50 cm, and the wave is 8/20 µs with an amplitude of 8 kÂ, the voltage across the equipment terminals will be Up + 500 V.

claim: Schneider Electrical Installation Guide: in a metal switchgear enclosure it may be wise to connect the SPD directly to the enclosure, using the enclosure as the protective conductor (the assembly manufacturer must confirm this per IEC 61439-2).
quote: In the case of a switchgear assembly in a metallic enclosure, it may be wise to connect the SPD directly to the metallic enclosure, with the enclosure being used as a protective conductor

claim: Schneider Electrical Installation Guide (IEC 60364): minimum SPD connection cross-section at the incoming end is 4 mm2 copper for a Type 2 SPD and 16 mm2 copper for a Type 1 SPD (lightning protection system present).
